title: POVERTY & INEQUALITY UPDATE
text:
Global poverty reduction has slowed to a near standstill, with 2020–2030 set to be a lost decade. Almost half the world’s population – approximately 3.5 billion people – are living on less than $6.85 a day, the poverty line for upper-middle-income countries. Almost

700 million people are living in extreme poverty, trying to survive on less than $2.15 a day, the poverty line for low-income countries. About three-quarters of all people in extreme poverty live in Sub-Saharan Africa and/or places impacted by conflict and fragility.

Progress has stalled amid multiple crises and shocks, impacting low-income countries the hardest and preventing the poorest people from catching up. This polycrisis includes slow economic growth, increased conflict and fragility, persistent inequality, high indebtedness, and climate shocks.

Gains in reducing the Global Prosperity Gap, the World Bank’s new measure of shared prosperity, have also paused since the COVID-19 pandemic. Today, incomes around the world, on average, would have to increase five-fold to reach a prosperity standard of $25 per person per day.

#### PROGRESS: GLOBAL POVERTY REDUCTION

#### AND IMPROVEMENTS IN SHARED PROSPERITY HAVE STALLED SKU 212123

The Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2024 is the latest edition of the series formerly known as Poverty and Shared Prosperity. The report emphasizes that reducing poverty and increasing shared prosperity must be achieved in ways that do not come at unacceptably high costs to the environment. The current “polycrisis”—where the multiple crises of slow economic growth, increased fragility, climate risks, and heightened uncertainty have come together at the same time—makes national development strategies and international cooperation difficult. Offering the first post-COVID-19 pandemic assessment of global progress on this interlinked agenda, the report finds that global poverty reduction has resumed but at a pace slower than before the Coronavirus crisis. Nearly 700 million people worldwide live in extreme poverty with less than US$2.15 per person per day. Progress has essentially plateaued amid lower economic growth and the impacts of COVID-19 and other crises. Today, extreme poverty is concentrated mostly in Sub-Saharan Africa and fragile settings. At a higher standard more typical of upper middle-income countries—US$6.85 per person per day—almost one-half of the world is living in poverty. The report also provides evidence that the number of countries that have high levels of income inequality has declined considerably during the past two decades, but the pace of improvements in shared prosperity has slowed, and that inequality remains high in Latin America and the Caribbean and Sub-Saharan Africa. Worldwide, people’s incomes today would need to increase fivefold to reach a minimum prosperity threshold of US$25 per person per day. Where there has been progress in poverty reduction and shared prosperity, there is evidence of an increasing ability of countries to manage natural hazards, but climate risks are significantly higher in the poorest settings. Nearly one in five people globally is at risk of experiencing welfare losses due to an extreme weather event from which they will struggle to recover. The interconnected issues of climate change and poverty call for a united and inclusive effort from the global community. Development cooperation stakeholders—from governments, nongovernmental organizations, and the private sector to communities and citizens acting locally in every corner of the globe—hold pivotal roles in promoting fair and sustainable transitions. By emphasizing strategies that yield multiple benefits and diligently monitoring and addressing trade-offs, we can strive toward a future that is prosperous, equitable, and resilient.

PATHWAYS OUT OF THE POLYCRISIS

P O V E R T Y, P R O S P E R I T Y, AND PLANET REPORT 2024

### PATHWAYS OUT OF THE POLYCRISIS

## POVERTY & INEQUALITY UPDATE

FALL 2024

SPECIAL EDITION

The Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2024 offers the first postpandemic assessment of global progress toward ending poverty and boosting shared prosperity on a livable planet, and explores potential pathways out of today’s polycrisis.

Around one-fifth of the world’s population lives in countries with high inequality. High inequality reflects a lack of 
opportunity for socioeconomic mobility, which can further hinder prospects for poverty reduction and shared prosperity. 
Climate change poses a fundamental threat to poverty and inequality reduction. Nearly one in five people are at 
high risk of experiencing welfare losses due to an extreme weather event from which they will struggle to recover. Being at 
high risk is defined as being exposed to climate-related hazards and also being vulnerable to their impacts. 
In 2022, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reached record levels, trapping nearly 50% more heat than in 1990. 
This rise in temperatures due to GHG emissions will lead to more frequent and more intense extreme weather events, 
further threatening lives and livelihoods. 
Significant gaps in human capital, basic infrastructure, and life essentials affect large populations in the poorest 
regions. Millions of people, especially in Sub-Saharan Africa and in fragile and conflict-affected situations, lack access to 
sufficient health, nutrition and sanitation, housing, electricity, and education. 
Progress on the interlinked goals requires faster, inclusive growth and protecting people from extreme weather 
events. Enabling people in poverty to benefit more from economic growth requires better-functioning labor markets, 
alongside investments in people and their capacity to climb the socioeconomic ladder. 
With limited budgets, high uncertainty, and conflicting interests, policy makers must prioritize and make difficult 
choices. Policy makers must understand the trade-offs between growing incomes and lowering emissions, find ways to 
scale up synergistic policies that can accelerate equitable progress, and manage transition costs to specific groups and 
communities affected by labor market or price shifts. 
Actions need to recognize that richer countries generate the most emissions and that poorer countries are the 
most at risk. Whereas upper-middle- and high-income countries currently account for four-fifths of global GHG emissions, 
low- and lower-middle-income countries contribute a relatively small share of emissions, although they are home to one 
half of the world’s population. 
Advancing on the eradication of extreme poverty does not come at a big cost for the planet because the poorest 
countries contribute so little to emissions. Eradicating extreme poverty would increase emissions by less than 5% 
above 2019 levels. But eradicating poverty at the level more relevant for middle-income countries – that is, moving more 
than 3 billion people above $6.85 per day – would lead to a significant increase in emissions. 

#### PATHWAYS: ERADICATING POVERTY AND BOOSTING SHARED PROSPERITY ON A LIVABLE PLANET REQUIRES MANAGING TRADE-OFFS

Low-income and fragile countries need to prioritize poverty reduction by fostering investment in human, 
physical, and financial capital. IDA countries account for 7 in 10 of the global extreme poor today. Promoting higher, 
inclusive economic growth; basic investments; and insurance are fundamental to sustainably improve the lives of the poor. 
Middle-income countries must prioritize income growth that reduces vulnerability and pursue synergistic actions. 
Accelerating economic growth, enhancing the productive capacity of poorer households, and risk management are key. At 
the same time, without action, their emissions will increase over the next decades and surpass those of richer countries. 
High-income and upper-middle-income countries with high emissions must accelerate 
mitigation to advance on the interlinked goals globally while managing transition 
costs. Although emissions in those settings are projected to decline under current policies, 
progress is not nearly fast enough to limit global warming. 
Advancing on these interlinked global challenges requires a solid foundation 
of evidence. We need more and better data to address these complex policy issues 
and monitor impacts. This requires stronger national statistical systems and innovative 
approaches to advance the frontier of data and modeling for welfare analysis. 
Urgent and coordinated global action is essential to meet these interlinked goals. 
The financing gap for sustainable development is growing. Countries need to focus and 
prioritize the actions that will have the highest return for development. Ending poverty and 
boosting shared prosperity on a livable planet will require a new global social contract. 

#### PRIORITIES: DOING WHAT MATTERS WHERE IT MATTERS
